title: Filters and Ultrafilters: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: For every nonempty $C\subseteq X$, the supersets of $C$ form the filter generated by $\{C\}$, and this filter is an ultrafilter exactly when $C$ is a singleton
items.strategy: Check the filter axioms directly, identify it with the upward closure from the filter-base construction, and use the complement characterisation to prove the singleton criterion.

items.title: The subsets of $X$ containing a fixed point $x$ form the principal ultrafilter at $x$
items.strategy: Specialise the preceding principal-filter computation to $C=\{x\}$ and verify the complement dichotomy.

items.title: The subsets of $\mathbb N$ containing a tail form the Fréchet filter, and it is proper and not an ultrafilter
items.strategy: Use tails $T_k=\{n\in\mathbb N:k\le n\}$ as a filter base. Their generated filter is proper; the even and odd subsets witness failure of the ultrafilter dichotomy. Explain that this is the cofinite filter on $\mathbb N$, proving the tail/cofinite agreement rather than assuming it.

items.title: An ultrafilter extending the Fréchet filter on $\mathbb N$ is free, and its existence uses the ultrafilter lemma
items.strategy: Extend the Fréchet filter by the ultrafilter lemma. No singleton belongs to the extension because its complementary tail does, so the extension cannot be principal. State the choice cost explicitly.

items.title: An ultrafilter containing the union of a finite list of pairwise disjoint sets contains exactly one nonempty cell
items.strategy: Induct on the length of the list using the finite-union form of ultrafilter primeness; uniqueness follows because two disjoint members would force the empty set into the filter. The list is indexed by a natural number, so no later finite-cardinality machinery is used.

items.title: The union of the two principal ultrafilters on a two-point set is not a filter
items.strategy: The union contains both singleton subsets, while closure under intersections would require the empty set. Contrast arbitrary unions with unions of chains.

items.title: The intersection of the two principal ultrafilters on a two-point set is a filter but not an ultrafilter
items.strategy: Compute the intersection as the one-member filter $\{X\}$ and exhibit a singleton whose two complementary cells are both absent.

items.title: If the exclusion of $\varnothing$ is dropped, $\mathcal P(X)$ becomes the unique maximal improper filter
items.strategy: Show that upward and finite-intersection closure plus membership of the empty set force every subset into the family; explain why this object is excluded by the library's proper-filter convention.

title: Congruences, the Integers Modulo n and the Chinese Remainder Theorem

items.title: Congruence modulo an integer: $a\equiv b\pmod n$ when $n\mid(a-b)$, including the moduli $0$ and $1$
Congruence modulo every integer is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Unfold divisibility for reflexivity and use sign invariance and linearity for symmetry and transitivity. Record that modulus $0$ gives equality and modulus $1$ gives the universal relation.

items.title: Congruent integers may be added, subtracted and multiplied: representative changes preserve both arithmetic operations
items.strategy: For multiplication expand $ab-a'b'=a(b-b')+b'(a-a')$ and apply divisibility linearity. Include the unary-negation and integer-power consequences.

items.title: The congruence class $[a]_n$ and the quotient set $\mathbb Z/n$
For $n\ge 1$, every class in $\mathbb Z/n$ has one representative $r$ with $0\le r<n$, so $\lvert\mathbb Z/n\rvert=n$; while $\mathbb Z/0$ is in bijection with $\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use division with remainder for existence and uniqueness. Construct the bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to the quotient. Treat $n=1$ and $n=0$ explicitly.

items.title: Addition and multiplication on $\mathbb Z/n$ by $[a]_n+[b]_n=[a+b]_n$ and $[a]_n[b]_n=[ab]_n$
items.strategy: Representative independence is licensed by the preceding compatibility lemma. State that these are binary operations for every natural modulus, including $0$ and $1$.

items.title: For every natural $n$, $(\mathbb Z/n,+)$ is an abelian group, multiplication is a commutative monoid operation, and both distributive laws hold
items.strategy: Transfer each identity from the commutative ring of integers through representatives. Record additive inverses as $[-a]_n$ and the two identities as $[0]_n$ and $[1]_n$, which coincide when $n=1$.

items.title: The unit group $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ and Euler's totient $\varphi(n)=\lvert(\mathbb Z/n)^\times\rvert$ for $n\ge1$
items.strategy: Take the invertible elements of the multiplicative monoid and use the published unit-group lemma. Finiteness follows because the unit set is a subset of the finite quotient. Fix $\varphi(1)=1$ from the one-element monoid, not by a separate convention.

items.title: For $n\ge1$, $[a]_n$ is a unit if and only if $\gcd(a,n)=1$
items.strategy: A Bézout identity gives an inverse. Conversely an inverse gives $ab+nk=1$, so every common divisor divides $1$. Verify representative independence of the gcd-one condition.

items.title: $\varphi(1)=1$, and $\varphi(p)=p-1$ for every prime $p$
items.strategy: For a prime, every nonzero standard representative is coprime to $p$ and the zero class is not. Include the one-element modulus as a separate first clause.

items.title: For a prime $p$ and $k\ge1$, multiplication by $p$ bijects the standard representatives modulo $p^{k-1}$ with the representatives modulo $p^k$ divisible by $p$
items.strategy: Use the power recursion and integer cancellation to prove injectivity and the division witness to prove surjectivity. Keep natural exponents in the published monoid-power sense.

items.title: For a prime $p$ and $k\ge1$, $\varphi(p^k)=p^k-p^{k-1}$
items.strategy: The nonunits among the standard representatives are exactly the multiples of $p$. Count them by the preceding bijection and subtract from the full residue set.

items.title: If $n\ge1$, $d=\gcd(a,n)$ and $d\mid b$, then $ax\equiv b\pmod n$ reduces to a congruence with coprime coefficient modulo $n/d$
items.strategy: Write $a=da'$, $n=dn'$, $b=db'$ and cancel nonzero $d$ in the divisibility equation. Cite the published theorem that $a'$ and $n'$ are coprime.

items.title: For $n\ge1$, $ax\equiv b\pmod n$ is solvable exactly when $\gcd(a,n)\mid b$, and then has exactly $\gcd(a,n)$ solution classes modulo $n$
items.strategy: Necessity is divisibility of a linear combination. For sufficiency reduce by the gcd and use Bézout. Parameterise the solutions by adding multiples of $n/d$ and prove the resulting $d$ classes are distinct and exhaustive.

items.title: For a finite pairwise-coprime list of positive integers, the product divides every common multiple, and each initial product is coprime to every remaining modulus
items.strategy: Induct on list length, repeatedly applying the coprime-divides-product lemma. The second clause supplies the induction seam for the finite Chinese remainder theorem.

items.title: For coprime positive $m,n$, every pair of residue classes modulo $m$ and $n$ has a unique simultaneous class modulo $mn$
items.strategy: Use Bézout coefficients to construct a solution and the coprime-divisibility lemma for uniqueness modulo $mn$. Include the cases $m=1$ or $n=1$.

items.title: Chinese remainder theorem for a finite pairwise-coprime list: simultaneous residues determine one class modulo the product, and the resulting bijection preserves addition and multiplication
items.strategy: Induct using the two-modulus lemma and the initial-product coprimality clause. Prove the map and its inverse are well defined, then check preservation of both operations componentwise. At an empty list the product is $1$ and both sides are one-element sets.

items.title: Euler's totient is multiplicative: $\gcd(m,n)=1$ implies $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$ for positive $m,n$
items.strategy: Restrict the CRT bijection to unit groups using the componentwise unit criterion, then apply the product rule for finite cardinalities.

items.title: Euler's product formula $\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}(1-1/p)=\prod_{p^k\parallel n}(p^k-p^{k-1})$ for $n\ge1$, stated through a finite injective list of its prime divisors
items.strategy: Use inclusion-exclusion on the standard representatives divisible by each distinct prime divisor. An intersection indexed by $J$ has size $n/\prod_{j\in J}p_j$. Translate the alternating sum to the finite product; state the formula without an infinite-product notation. Give the CRT/prime-power route as a second proof in a Remark, not as a duplicate theorem.

items.title: For every positive integer $n$, $\sum_{d\mid n,\ d>0}\varphi(d)=n$
items.strategy: Partition the standard representatives modulo $n$ by the value of $n/\gcd(a,n)$. The block indexed by a positive divisor $d$ is in bijection with $(\mathbb Z/d)^\times$. Prove the positive-divisor index set finite and use the finite sum rule.

items.title: For every prime $p$, the two operations on $\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field
items.strategy: Use the basic algebra theorem for all additive, multiplicative and distributive axioms. Every nonzero class has representative not divisible by $p$, hence is a unit. Verify $[0]_p\ne[1]_p$ from $p>1$.

items.title: In $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, inversion pairs every class except $[1]_p$ and $[-1]_p$, which are the only self-inverse classes
items.strategy: A self-inverse class satisfies $(x-1)(x+1)=0$ in the field $\mathbb Z/p$; multiply by inverses to obtain one factor zero. Pair all remaining elements with distinct inverses, handling $p=2$ separately.

items.title: Wilson's theorem: for every prime $p$, $(p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p$
items.strategy: Multiply all nonzero residue classes. The inverse pairs contribute the identity and the two self-inverse classes contribute $-1$. Identify the product of standard representatives with $(p-1)!$, including $p=2$.

title: Congruences and Modular Arithmetic: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The system $x\equiv2\pmod3$, $x\equiv3\pmod5$, $x\equiv2\pmod7$ has the unique solution $x\equiv23\pmod{105}$
items.strategy: Construct the solution with Bézout idempotents and verify all three congruences and uniqueness modulo the product.

items.title: The congruence $14x\equiv30\pmod{100}$ has exactly the two solutions $x\equiv45,95\pmod{100}$
items.strategy: Compute the gcd, reduce to $7x\equiv15\pmod{50}$, find the inverse of $7$, and list the two lifts modulo $100$.

items.title: $(\mathbb Z/12)^\times=\{[1],[5],[7],[11]\}$ and $\varphi(12)=4$
items.strategy: List the standard representatives coprime to $12$, compute their inverses, and check the product formula $(4-2)(3-1)=4$.

items.title: The Chinese remainder bijection $\mathbb Z/12\to\mathbb Z/3\times\mathbb Z/4$ computed on all standard representatives
items.strategy: Tabulate $[a]_{12}\mapsto([a]_3,[a]_4)$, then check addition and multiplication on representative nontrivial pairs.

items.title: $(\mathbb Z/8)^\times=\{[1],[3],[5],[7]\}$ is not cyclic because every element squares to $[1]$
items.strategy: List the units by the gcd criterion and square each class. A cyclic group of four elements would have an element of order four.

items.title: $\varphi(360)=96$ by both inclusion-exclusion and the prime-power product formula
items.strategy: Use $360=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5$ and compute the two forms term by term, making their equality explicit.

items.title: The system $x\equiv1\pmod2$, $x\equiv2\pmod4$ has no solution, so coprimality in the Chinese remainder theorem cannot be dropped
items.strategy: The second congruence forces $x$ even and the first forces $x$ odd. Identify the failed compatibility condition modulo the gcd.

items.title: A modulus $n>1$ is composite exactly when two nonzero classes in $\mathbb Z/n$ have product $[0]_n$
items.strategy: A factorisation $n=ab$ with $1<a,b<n$ gives the two classes. Conversely lift a zero product of nonzero classes, use the unit criterion to find a nontrivial gcd, and obtain a nontrivial divisor of $n$.

items.title: False: $[a]_n[b]_n=[0]_n$ always implies $[a]_n=[0]_n$ or $[b]_n=[0]_n$
items.strategy: Refute at $n=6$ with $[2]_6[3]_6=[0]_6$, while both factors have nonzero standard representatives.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/1$ has one element and satisfies $[0]_1=[1]_1$, so it is not a field
items.strategy: Compute the quotient and cite the distinct-zero-and-one clause in the field definition.

items.title: Intervals in a poset; locally finite, lower-finite and upper-finite posets
items.strategy: Define $[x,y]=\{z:x\le z\le y\}$. Locally finite means every such interval is finite; lower-finite and upper-finite mean every principal ideal and principal filter is finite. State that either one-sided condition implies local finiteness.

items.title: A finite sum in a commutative monoid indexed by an arbitrary finite set
items.strategy: Enumerate the finite index set, use the monoid finite-product construction in additive notation, and prove independence of the enumeration from generalised commutativity. Record agreement with the published real- and natural-valued finite-index-set sum.

items.title: Finite commutative-monoid sums are invariant under bijective reindexing, split over disjoint unions, and satisfy the finite Fubini rule
items.strategy: Reduce reindexing to permutation invariance, disjoint unions to concatenated enumerations, and the double sum to an enumeration of the finite Cartesian product.

items.title: The incidence functions $I(P,R)$ of a locally finite poset and their convolution
items.strategy: For a locally finite poset $P$ and commutative ring $R$, define functions on comparable pairs and $(f*g)(x,y)=\sum_{x\le z\le y}f(x,z)g(z,y)$. Local finiteness and the general finite-sum definition make the operation well defined.

items.title: The delta and zeta incidence functions
items.strategy: Define $\delta(x,y)=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\zeta(x,y)=1$ on every comparable pair.

items.title: Incidence convolution is associative and distributes over pointwise addition
items.strategy: Expand both bracketings as the same finite sum over pairs $x\le u\le v\le y$, using finite Fubini and bijective reindexing. Prove both distributive laws termwise.

items.title: Pointwise addition and convolution make $I(P,R)$ a ring with identity $\delta$
items.strategy: Obtain the pointwise additive abelian group from the function-ring construction, use the preceding lemma for multiplication and distributivity, and compute $\delta*f=f=f*\delta$.

items.title: If every diagonal value of an incidence function is a unit, recursive interval formulas construct both a left and a right convolution inverse
items.strategy: Use strong induction on the finite cardinality of $[x,y]$. Solve the equations $(f*g)(x,y)=0$ and $(h*f)(x,y)=0$ off the diagonal after isolating the diagonal unit. Then $h=h*(f*g)=(h*f)*g=g$, so the one-sided inverses coincide.

items.title: An incidence function is convolution-invertible if and only if every diagonal value is a unit
items.strategy: Necessity follows by evaluating an inverse equation on $(x,x)$. Sufficiency is the recursive construction. State the criterion for arbitrary locally finite $P$, including infinite $P$.

items.title: The integer-valued Möbius function $\mu_P$ of a locally finite poset
items.strategy: Take the inverse of the zeta function in $I(P,\mathbb Z)$. Existence and uniqueness come from the invertibility criterion because every diagonal value is $1$. This fixes the coefficient ring as $\mathbb Z$ and avoids a characteristic-dependent second notion.

items.title: The Möbius recurrence: $\mu_P(x,x)=1$ and both interval sums of $\mu_P$ vanish when $x<y$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\mu*\zeta=\delta$ and $\zeta*\mu=\delta$. Isolate the endpoint term to obtain the two recursive formulas and uniqueness.

items.title: Möbius inversion on a lower-finite poset, with the dual upper-finite form
items.strategy: For functions $f,g:P\to R$ into a commutative ring, prove $g(y)=\sum_{x\le y}f(x)$ iff $f(y)=\sum_{x\le y}\mu_P(x,y)g(x)$. Interchange the finite double sum and use the recurrence. State and prove the order-dual upper-finite form separately.

items.title: Both forms of Möbius inversion hold on every finite poset
items.strategy: Every principal ideal and filter is a subset of the finite ground set, hence finite; apply both halves of the preceding theorem.

items.title: The Möbius function of a product poset is the product of the Möbius functions
items.strategy: Show intervals in $P\times Q$ are Cartesian products of intervals and hence finite. Verify that the proposed product satisfies the Möbius recurrence using finite Fubini.

items.title: For $A\subseteq B$ in a finite Boolean lattice, $\mu(A,B)=(-1)^{\lvert B\setminus A\rvert}$
items.strategy: Identify the interval $[A,B]$ with a product of two-element chains indexed by $B\setminus A$, then apply the product theorem. Alternatively verify the recurrence by the alternating binomial sum; keep one route as the proof and the other as a Remark.

items.title: The complementary inclusion-exclusion formula is Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
items.strategy: Index intersections by subsets of the sieve index set, apply finite-poset Möbius inversion, insert the Boolean-lattice formula, and match every term and sign to the published complementary sieve identity.

items.title: On a finite chain, the Möbius function is $1$ on the diagonal, $-1$ on covers and $0$ on longer intervals
items.strategy: Induct on interval cardinality using the recurrence. The first nontrivial interval gives $-1$ and every longer interval has partial sum $1-1=0$ before the final term.

items.title: The divisibility poset of positive integers
items.strategy: Restrict integer divisibility to positive integers and verify reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity. Its interval $[a,b]$ consists of the positive integers $d$ with $a\mid d\mid b$.

items.title: The divisibility poset is lower-finite, and each divisor interval factorises as a product of finite chains of prime exponents
items.strategy: Positive divisors of $n$ lie in a finite initial segment. Use canonical prime factorisation and valuations to biject divisors with exponent tuples $0\le e_i\le v_{p_i}(n)$, preserving and reflecting divisibility.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function $\mu(n)$ from prime factorisation
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$, set $\mu(n)=0$ when some prime square divides $n$, and $\mu(n)=(-1)^r$ when $n$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes. Use uniqueness of prime factorisation to prove $r$ and the value are well defined, including $\mu(1)=1$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is the poset Möbius function of divisibility: $\mu(n)=\mu_{\mid}(1,n)$
items.strategy: Use the prime-exponent product decomposition of the divisor interval, the product theorem and the finite-chain formula. A repeated prime exponent contributes zero; otherwise every nontrivial chain contributes $-1$.

items.title: Classical Möbius inversion over positive divisors
items.strategy: Apply lower-finite poset inversion to the divisibility order and substitute the agreement theorem. Give both standard equivalent indexings, with $\mu(d)$ and with $\mu(n/d)$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is multiplicative on coprime positive integers
items.strategy: For coprime $m,n$, divisors of $mn$ split uniquely into a divisor of $m$ and a divisor of $n$ by prime factorisation. Apply the product-poset theorem and the agreement theorem.

items.title: False: convolution defines an incidence algebra for every poset
items.strategy: Refute with the companion's poset having an infinite interval: convolution of the constant-one functions asks for an infinite sum not defined by the ring axioms.

items.title: False: $\mu_P(x,y)$ depends only on the cardinality of $[x,y]$
items.strategy: Compare a four-element chain, whose endpoint value is $0$, with the four-element diamond, whose endpoint value is $1$.

items.title: False: classical Möbius inversion and inclusion-exclusion are unrelated inversion principles
items.strategy: Refute by citing their common finite-poset inversion theorem and the two dictionary results for the divisibility and Boolean posets.

title: Incidence Algebras and Möbius Inversion — Examples

items.title: The full Möbius table of the Boolean lattice $2^{[3]}$
items.strategy: List comparable pairs by rank difference and assign $1,-1,1,-1$ according to the Boolean-lattice formula, checking representative recurrence sums.

items.title: The Möbius table of a four-element chain
items.strategy: Compute recursively: diagonal entries are $1$, cover entries are $-1$, and all entries spanning at least two covers are $0$.

items.title: The Möbius function on the divisor poset of $12$ and its agreement with $\mu(1),\mu(2),\mu(3),\mu(4),\mu(6),\mu(12)$
items.strategy: Draw the divisor order, compute from the recurrence, and compare each value with the prime-factor definition.

items.title: The endpoint Möbius value of the four-element diamond is $1$
items.strategy: Compute the two cover values as $-1$, then solve $1-1-1+\mu(\bot,\top)=0$.

items.title: Möbius inversion of $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$ gives $\varphi(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)(n/d)$
items.strategy: Apply classical Möbius inversion to the totient divisor-sum theorem and verify the formula numerically at $n=12$.

items.title: A poset with a bottom, a top and countably many incomparable middle elements has an infinite interval, so convolution of constant-one functions is not defined
items.strategy: Use the tagged set $\{\bot,\top\}\cup(\mathbb N\times\{m\})$, with every middle element strictly between the endpoints. The endpoint convolution sum has one term for each middle element.

items.title: On a two-element chain, an incidence function with a zero diagonal value is not convolution-invertible
items.strategy: Set $f(0,0)=0$ and evaluate any purported inverse equation on $(0,0)$; the diagonal product remains zero rather than one.

items.title: A four-element chain and a four-element diamond have equal-size endpoint intervals but Möbius values $0$ and $1$
items.strategy: Place the two preceding computations side by side and identify the different internal order structures that change the recurrence.
